new_statements.quote: 3.4 Tone Gura appears to have two level tones plus a single falling tone. Occasionally a phonetic mid-tone was recorded, so these have been left in the dataset, but these may be downsteps or similar phenomena. Some examples of tonal contrast; sú we/us sù spoil rò to wake up rô village kà to drip kâ here [...] kósó lizard kòsò basket túrù to pound tùrú sleep
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger M. & Timothy Terna. 2024. An introduction to Gura [bma], a previously undocumented Jarawan Bantu language of Central Nigeria. Working document, Kay Williamson Educational Foundation, Cambridge / University of Jos, dated 15 September 2024.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 3.4 Tone, p. 4 (main text); orthography remark sec. 5, p. 12
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only published description treats Gura (the living variety of Lame) as a two-level-tone language (H, L) with a falling contour and sporadic phonetic mid tones read as downstep; lexical tone is contrastive on monosyllables and disyllables. The source says nothing at all about word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress rule can be stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: occasional phonetic mid tones 'may be downsteps or similar phenomena'; 'There is so far no reason to mark tone in the orthography, but this may change with further research.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on citation forms from a preliminary elicited dataset (draft lexicon); no phrase-level or instrumental data. Blench & Terna call the analysis 'obviously preliminary'.
new_statements.identity_note: The only description (Blench & Terna 2024) covers Gura, which Glottolog files as a dialect of Lame [gura1253 under lame1257] and Ethnologue/Wikipedia list as one of three Lame varieties (Rufu/Ruhu and Mbaru reported extinct since 1987). Blench's own classification tree (2024 Fig. 1; 2026 slides) treats Gura, Lame, Mbaru and Ruhu as separate Nigerian Jarawan Bantu nodes, and the document itself says 'Gura (ISO bma; glottocode gura1253)'. Any catalog entry should be keyed to gura1253 / labelled 'Gura variety of Lame'.

sources.note: Sec. 3 Phonology (pp. 3-4) covers consonants, labialisation/palatalisation, six vowels with length, and 3.4 Tone: two level tones plus one falling tone, occasional phonetic mid tone read as downstep. Orthography section: no reason yet to mark tone. The words stress/accent/prominence do not occur anywhere in the main text (secs 1-6, references). Full main text embedded in the Wayback 2025-08-02 capture of the Academia.edu page; PDF itself login-gated.
Dialects Rufu, Mbaru, Gura; Rufu and Mbaru extinct as of 1987; cites Blench 2025 Gura introduction and Gura dictionary on Academia.edu (used only to locate them).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2026. The Jarawan Bantu languages in Nigeria; what is new research telling us? Jos Linguistic Circle slides, 15 July 2026 (Academia.edu 170218202).
sources.note: Gura slides: 'TONES Gura has two level tones plus a falling tone. Occasionally a mid-tone was recorded, which is interpreted as downstep or upstep.' Nothing on stress. Classification tree lists Ruhu, Lame, Mbaru and Gura as separate nodes under Nigerian Jarawan Bantu.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2019. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, ed. IV. Cambridge: KWEF. Entry 283 'Lame cluster' (*Ruhu, *Mbaru, *Gura).
sources.note: Location (Toro LGA, Lame district), 2,000 (1973 SIL); Ruhu no speakers 1987; Mbaru 3500-4500 (CAPRO 1995a); Gura names Tu-Gura, Ba-/Mo-Gura, Agari, Agbiri. Refs: Shimizu (1983). No phonology.
